newsitem.title: PERU: Peru expects peaceful end to hostage crisis.
newsitem.headline: Peru expects peaceful end to hostage crisis.

text.p: Peruvian Prime Minister Alberto Pandolfi said on Monday he expected the siege at the Japanese ambassador's residence to end with the 83 remaining hostages released unharmed by their Marxist captors.

"We are sure that the continuing sound handling of the situation will allow a solution that protects the physical well-being and lives of all of the hostages," the head of the government's cabinet said in a speech.
"The government is working permanently with prudence and dedication for the prompt release" of the hostages, he added, without giving more details.

There has been no word for nine days from President Alberto Fujimori, whose only public reaction to the seizure of the residence came in a blunt, two-minute speech in which he pledged not to use force if the hostage takers laid down arms.

Sources close to Fujimori said on Monday that the president, who has the final say on important matters, had held frequent meetings with the government's security adviser, Valdimiro Montesinos, since the Dec. 17 raid on the residence.
A shadowy and controversial figure, Montesinos has played a key role in cracking down on Peru's left-wing guerrillas since Fujimori won elections in 1990.

The prime minister's confident statement on ending the crisis reflected a new mood of hope since the first face-to-face meeting on Saturday between the guerrillas in the residence and government negotiator Domingo Palermo, who was picked for the job by Fujimori.
The meeting between Palermo, who is minister of education in Fujimori's cabinet, and rebel chief Nestor Cerpa Cartolini resulted in the release of 20 more hostages.

By Monday afternoon, there had been no further initiatives from the roughly 20 rebels. Heavily armed with grenades and automatic rifles, they have booby-trapped and mined the residence in Lima's fashionable San Isidro district.

But in a move some diplomats saw as an attempt by the guerrillas to portray themselves as respectable negotiating partners, the international spokesman of the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) condemned a "solidarity" bomb attack on the Peruvian embassy in Athens.
A group identifying itself as the Guerrilla Fighting Group claimed credit for the attack, in which one woman was injured.
"We reject this sort of display of solidarity because it does not contribute to the solution of a crisis," MRTA spokesman Isaac Velazco told Reuters in a telephone interview from Hamburg, Germany.
"We do not justify violence for the sake of violence," he said. "Solidarity has to be expressed within the negotiating process."
Earlier on Monday, hostages trapped at the besieged ambassador's home sent letters to families -- the first correspondence allowed out in four days.

Relatives of the captives, suffering their 13th day under rebel guns, went to Red Cross headquarters in Lima to pick up scores of messages scrawled on special forms provided by the organisation. Red Cross officials also took food and supplies to the residence.
The family of Jesuit priest Juan Julio Wicht, who is among the captives, released a letter he wrote over Christmas.
The priest jovially boasted that he was unbeaten at chess after eight games with Japanese and Peruvian diplomats.

"I am well and I am doing a lot of good for everyone here in such difficult circumstances," wrote Wicht, who opted to stay in the residence despite being offered freedom. He has celebrated various Masses for the captives.
"I am here on a mission and I feel your support and prayers ... I am simply doing what any of you or any Jesuit would do, but better than I."

He said tensions were rising and nights spent on the floor of the house were long and hot. But "we hostages maintain our unity and spirits, we pray together and we sing although we do not have the words ... God is helping us."
The remaining hostages include Fujimori's brother Pedro, top Peruvian police and government officials and about 20 Japanese businessmen.

As the New Year approached, police and civil leaders called on Peruvians to tone down celebrations in sympathy with the hostages, and to refrain from using fireworks -- particularly around the residence -- so as not to alarm the rebels.

Despite the hopes for a peaceful resolution to the crisis, Peruvian anti-terrorism police sources said crack troops had completed their preparations for a possible assault on the residence if needed as a last resort.
